questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme and stanza structure of a Shakespearean sonnet?
questions.a: A Shakespearean sonnet consists of three quatrains (four-line stanzas) followed by a final couplet (two lines), with the rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. A wrong answer (e.g., ABBA ABBA CDE CDE) reveals confusion with the Petrarchan sonnet form, indicating the student has not distinguished between the two major sonnet traditions — a critical gap for analyzing why Shakespeare chose this structure for his argument about love.

questions.q: Why might a poet choose to define something by stating what it is NOT (using negatives) rather than what it is?
questions.a: Using negatives (e.g., "Love is not love / Which alters...") creates a process of elimination that narrows the definition to an absolute ideal, making the positive assertion ("It is an ever-fixed mark") more forceful by contrast. It also mimics legal or philosophical argumentation, establishing the speaker's authority. A wrong answer that merely says "for emphasis" misses the logical and rhetorical strategy: the negatives systematically dismantle false versions of love to isolate the true one, which is central to the poem's argumentative structure.

questions.q: If you were to write a quatrain in Shakespearean sonnet form about friendship that mirrors the logical structure of the first quatrain of Sonnet 116, what would be the rhyme scheme and the pattern of argument?
questions.a: The quatrain would follow ABAB rhyme scheme. The argument pattern: Line 1 states the ideal ("Let me not to the friendship of true hearts / Admit obstacles"), Line 2 defines by negative ("Friendship is not friendship / Which changes when it alteration finds"), Line 3 extends the negative ("Or bends with the remover to remove"), Line 4 concludes the negative definition. A wrong answer that only focuses on rhyme without the logical progression (statement → negative definition → extension) shows the student sees form as decorative rather than functional — a senior-secondary error.

questions.q: Compare the two central metaphors in the poem — the "ever-fixed mark" (lighthouse) and the "star" (Polaris) — in terms of what each conveys about love's nature that the other does not.
questions.a: The "ever-fixed mark" (lighthouse) suggests love as a human-made, stationary guide that withstands storms (tempests) — emphasizing reliability and endurance. The "star" (Polaris) suggests a natural, celestial, distant guide whose "worth's unknown, although his height be taken" — emphasizing love's immeasurable value and universal constancy beyond human measurement. Together they cover both steadfastness and transcendence. A wrong answer that treats them as mere decoration misses how the metaphors complement each other: one earthly/active, one heavenly/passive, jointly constructing love as both accessible guide and absolute standard.

questions.q: Is the poet's claim in the final couplet — "If this be error, and upon me proved, / I never writ, nor no man ever loved" — a logically sound defense of his definition, or a rhetorical trap? Justify your evaluation.
questions.a: It is a rhetorical trap, not a logical proof. By staking his entire literary reputation and the universal human experience of love on his definition, Shakespeare makes disagreement practically impossible: to disprove him, one must prove either he didn't write (false) or no one has ever truly loved (absurd). This shifts the burden of proof impossibly high. A wrong answer that calls it "logical" confuses rhetorical force with logical validity — a common senior-secondary error when students conflate persuasive devices with philosophical argument.

questions.q: Write a Shakespearean sonnet couplet (two lines, iambic pentameter, rhyming GG) that stakes your own reputation on a definition of a human value (e.g., courage, honesty, loyalty) in the same way Shakespeare does.
questions.a: Example: "If loyalty be false when tested sore, / I never stood for truth, nor friend swore more." A good answer maintains iambic pentameter (da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM), rhymes GG, and mirrors the conditional "If this be error... I never..." structure. A poor answer that ignores meter or rhyme, or writes a generic moral statement without the self-referential stakes, reveals the student hasn't internalized how the couplet's form enacts the poem's ultimate argument: the poet's identity is inseparable from the truth he declares.
